maintopic: SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 SALES TAX-PROPOSED SELECT COMMITTEE OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
to the last farthing. There is no question that in this respect the tax is inequitable and unfair. Then, it is exceedingly complex and costly. The number of officers, clerks and inspectors that are necessary even to get the measure of collection that we are getting now from this tax is very large, but if the law were administered with any degree of exactitude; if the tax were collected from all, the officials would be multiplied many times. It is only by simply ignoring a great many persons that the cost of adminstration is kept as low at it is.
I am not going to attempt this afternoon to demonstrate to the last point the soundness of my contention for a change in the tax.
I am asking for an inquiry; I only hope to give the House sufficient information to excite its curiosity, shall I say, to the extent that it will grant this request, or to bring from the government assurances that will answer the purpose.
Let me give two specific cases, Mr. Speaker, to illustrate my point. Take first the case of the leather business. First, the dealer in hides pays 2i per cent on the sale to the tanner. Then, the tanner, on his sale to the shoe manufacturer, is assessed 2i per cent, and the shoe manufacturer on his sale to the wholesaler is assessed 2i per cent, as well as the wholesaler on his sale to the retailer, or, in the case where the sale is made direct from the manufacturer to the retailer, there is a 4J per cent tax, which amounts to the same thing. There the tax ends; the pair of shoes goes out to the public; there is no further imposition. Now then, let us take a very similar case to show' how wholly unequal is the application of tic tax. Take the case of cocoa. The dealer fin cocoa beans, on his sale to the manufacturer, is assessed 2i per cent; then on the sale by the manufacturer of cocoa powder to the wholesaler, there is another 2| per cent. !On the sale by the wholesaler, of chocolate powder to the retailer there is another assessment of 2i per cent; or, as in the ease of the leather, if the manufacturer sells direct there is a 41- per cent tax, which is the same thing. Up to this point the application of the tax is the same in connection with these two industries; both are treated alike. But the retail purchaser of cocoa powder may be a manufacturer; in fact, the greater part of the candies, chocolates, and so on that are consumed is manufactured by persons or firms carrying on a retail business as well. The retailer who has paid the tax right down from the sale of cocoa beans to his own purchase becomes a manufacturer and is then assessed a 5 per cent manufacturing tax as well as the 4 V per cent sales tax. In order that it may be

clearly shown that I am not overstating the case, I have under my hand three specific instances taken from my own city which can be duplicated by scores of similar cases in every city throughout Canada. I will give these three cases to show the result of the application of this super-tax to the trade in question.
The Mission Confectionery Company, conducting a retail business in Vancouver, with very handsome retail stores, refreshment counters and cafe stalls, and at the same time manufacturing candies, paid in 1922 an amount in super-taxes-the tax I referred to a moment ago as being added to the amount that would be paid, say, by the shoe manufacturer -equal to the profit on the entire business for the year from the cafe bakery, confectionery and soda fountain. The only way they can carry on business is to have these various lines; they have their soda fountain; they serve light refreshments, cold soft drinks in the summer and hot drinks of various kinds in the winter. This service is a convenience to the public and is very widely patronized. A bakery and confectionery is also operated. That is one case. Here is another:	Chanticleer Limited paid in this super-tax in 1922 more than the profit on the entire business for the year, cafe included. In the case of R. C, Purdy, another large firm, the super-taxes for 1922 combined were greater than the profit in the entire business, cafe included, for 1921 and 1922 combined. These firms are threatened with annihilation if they must continue to pay this tax under the present system. It is not my purpose this afternoon to argue in detail regarding these particular cases. _ I merely cite them as illustrations of the inequity of this tax and the unfairness of its application, to show how under the present law one class of business will pay a given rate, while another class is called upon to pay a very much higher rate.
I have another illustration here. It is a letter from a dealer in furs and skins, from North Battleford. This man is just a jobber or broker who goes out into the country and buys furs and skins from the settlers and farmers. Sometimes he would buy, I suppose, lynx skins, wolf skins, or whatever the furbearing animals of the district might be sheep skins, cattle hides and so forth. He is a general dealer in skins. Such an individual serves a good purpose and is doing a useful work for the community. This man collects the skins in his locality, then when the big dealer comes along there is a sale tax upon this man who originally collected the skins. The big dealer certainly will not absorb that tax, and the result is that the small dealer has to absorb it, and naturally

it is an inconvenience and loss to his business, and in my estimation threatens to shut out a class of individual who is exceedingly useful to the community.
There are other phases of this question which I shall touch upon only very briefly; for instance, the application of this tax to such institutions as libraries and hospitals.
I' have resolutions under my hand which I shall not for a moment refer to other than to bring them to the attention of the committee as another reason for careful examination of the method of applying this tax.
Let me turn to another phase of this question. I want to suggest to the House that in place of the present system of collecting the sales tax from the manufacturer or dealer in raw material, from the manufacturer, the jobber or distributor, and then from the retailer, following this tax down through these various lines of business-and we exempt certain classes of goods, which increases the complexity of tha matter -instead of that I would suggest this simplified method of securing what I consider would certainly be quite as large a revenue. Take the present method we have of applying a certain excess duty, if you like to call it that, or sales tax duty of a given figure to be determined by a committee or by the government, as the case may be. Then impose a sales tax upon all manufacturers of manufactured goods which go to the public in a finished form. At the present time the manufactured article of one firm is in many cases the raw material of another, and there is your difficulty under the present system. You are taxing the man who purchases bar steel, for instance, to turn it into cutlery, though that bar steel is the finished product of the steel company. He pays the sales tax to the steel company, which offsets the duty in that case, but he has to reproduce that bar steel in the form of cutlery, and on that he pays a sales tax again. I might give innumerable illustrations of that kind. The present tax in its application is complex, intricate and to my mind wholly unnecessary. Therefore I suggest the imposition of this tax upon such manufacturers as produce an article finished for the ultimate consumer. That, X think, would give a very handsome revenue. You may say that it would be difficult to classify the manufacturers in that way. I do not think it would be. I remember during the war we had a licensing of all manufacturers as well as of other persons doing business, and certainly it would not require anything like the staff in connection with the minister's office
Special War Revenue Act
and throughout the country to register and license the manufacturers of Canada, who, after all, are the smallest body of classified business men. Of the three classes I have mentioned, manufacturers, wholesalers or jobbers, and retailers, the manufacturing group is the least numerous and necessarily the largest in their production both as tb value and quantity. Consequently, the imposition of the tax upon that group would minimize the cost of collection. Let the tax be of sufficient amount to raise the revenue. Then impose the excess duty to which I refer upon imports to offset such an imposition on the manufacturer.
In addition to that, I suggest that on all goods manufactured by such manufacturers, when exported or re-exported, as the case may be, there should be a rebate of such tax. The reason for that is that if our manufacturers are to compete in the world market they must be relieved from excess taxes in their own market. These taxes, we must remember, are imposed for the purpose of raising revenue to run the business of this country, and if our manufacturer is to compete in a foreign country and pay the import charges and taxes which are levied in that foreign country, such a tax as we suggest here, such a tax, in fact, as we are imposing to-day ought to be rebated on such goods as are exported or re-exported.
I do not wish to labour the question, I do not wish to go into detail. I have already intimated that my object is to bring to the attention of the House the fact that we have a very serious problem in connection, not only with this tax but every branch of taxation, but particularly in connection with this. I understand from figures given by those who are supposed to have sound information on the subject that we may expect from this sales tax a revenue to the amount of $90,000,000. This, will constitute a very large proportion of our revenue, and therefore inasmuch as this tax is affecting the whole of the business of Canada, it behooves us to give it the most exhaustive study as to whether or not this somewhat new tax is in any way interfering with the normal course of business.
It is claimed by the retailers particularly that it is working a severe hardship to-day. It is claimed by them, as I have already intimated, that the retailer who keeps an up-to-date set of books is penalized as compared with the retailer who does not keep books but just keeps slips of rough memoranda regarding his business transactions. It is exceedingly difficult to draw the line of demarcation between absolute fraud and mere ignorance on
91S

the part of small dealers. I am sure that those who have given any study to the question of accountancy will realize at once the absurdity of expecting a man down in the heart of any of our great cities, particularly the foreigner, who is doing in every other respect a legitimate business, and perhaps supplying a very great need in the community, to keep an accurate set of books when he is doing only a small business, such as many of them are doing to-day. So there is no use trying to kid ourselves, if I might be permitted to use that expression, into believing that it is possible to enforce the present tax to the point of exact equality and justice to all.
There are certain advantages which would accrue from the method of taxation I have suggested, and with a brief statement of them I shall take my seat. In the first place, it will reduce, and reduce enormously in my [DOT]opinion, the cost of collection. In the second place, it will eliminate this discrimination to which I have made very brief and altogether inadequate reference. In the third place, it will in my estimation bring a very much larger revenue to the exchequer of the country, a most desirable result at this time; and in the next place it will bring about a more equitable distribution of taxation over the country as a whole.
I am aware-and I pause for one moment to anticipate the point-that there are those who will at once apply to my suggestions the argument which has always applied to the imposition of a customs duty viz.-that it is always passed on to the consumer. Unquestionably it is passed on to the consumer. It makes no difference what form of tax is imposed it is ultimately passed on to the consumer. The error, however, that is often made in advancing that argument is that there is an imaginary line of demarcation drawn between consumers and others; that is, those who are sellers of goods-retailers, wholesalers or manufacturers-are often classified as being exempt from the penalties of the consumer. As a matter of fact everybody is a consumer, and there is no use trying to deceive ourselves. Taxes are always passed on to the consumer and will be, I care not what form they may take.
Let me illustrate the point very briefly: You may impose a tax, we will say, on the shoe manufacturer, and you may say with all the dignity and majesty of law that that tax must appear on the invoice, and that the shoe manufacturer must pay that tax. Certainly he will pay that tax, but if it puts him out of business he quits manufacturing. The only way he can continue to manufacture is I Mr. Stevens.]
to make a profit, over and above that tax, sufficient to induce him to continue in business; but if that tax so invades his profits as to make it unprofitable for him to continue he will quit manufacturing or, if he can, raise his price. So it does not make a whit of difference whether that tax does or does not appear on the invoice; it will be absorbed sooner or later by the ultimate purchaser and consumer.
There is another phase of the question to which I feel tempted to refer, and it is this: It is pretty generally admitted by those who are frank enough to do so, and I claim to be one of them, that the general public prefer to pay a tax that does not appear under their noses specified as a tax.

. Mr. STEVENS:* I think that is right; I think everyone who has had any experience with it at all will admit that. Now, I know that a great many pseudo economists who are very anxious to stir up discord will tell the consumer that this mysterious imposition of a tax in an intangible and undefined form has some criminal or some immoral taint about it. That, I think, is a fallacy, an utter fallacy. As a matter of fact business is very largely dependent upon the great general laws of supply and demand, and the question of whether a business is or is not a paying one; and the imposition of a tax-whether it is shown, as I said a moment ago, on the face of the invoice or whether it is absorbed in the general cost-in the long run makes no difference, except that it does cause a certain amount of irritation as has been proven beyond all peradventure in the United States and in Canada when we caused everybody who sold neckties, shirts, shoes, and such like articles, to show upon the counter slip the tax that went to the Dominion or to the federal government as the case might be. I do not think there was the slightest good-indeed I am convinced there was a great deal of irritation and harm-done by that. I have listened with much interest, and with a measure of sympathy, to the remarks of my hon. friend for Vancouver Centre, (Mr. Stevens) and I am quite sure he is moved entirely by a desire to meet some of the criticisms that we are familiar with from day to day on the sales tax-indeed as to other methods of taxation. It is a misfortune that the tremendous obligations of the war have obliged the government of the day, no matter what party may be in power, to discover new means of raising revenue; and it is quite possible that some of these new means are almost experimental in their character and that, in the light of experience, they may be modified or, in some cases possibly, abandoned altogether.
I am afraid that neither my hon. friend nor I can indulge in the hope of devising any means of taxation that will be popular. Taxation is not popular. New taxation is particularly objectionable. If your taxation has been in force for a number of years, even though it may seem to be inequitable, the people get accustomed to it and gradually cease to complain of it, but new taxes always bring forth a new cry against them, and that is the situation regarding the sales tax. The machinery of the sales tax is substantially the same as it was from the beginning. It has been changed somewhat in detail, and the amount has been increased; but it is a difficult thing to adjust. The cases to which my hon. friend has referred, as between the various branches of industry, certainly seem to make out a fair claim to consideration. The imposition of taxes, however, in the end must be the obligation and the responsibility of the government. There is no escape from that, and such being the case I can give my hon. friend assurance at once that what he has said, and other representations that we may receive on the subject, will be considered with the utmost desire to meet criticisms as far as possible.
I must not hold out the hope that we can reduce taxation to any considerable extent. It is a misfortune that we have to pay high taxes-but every country in the world has to pay them too-and there is naturally a desire for exemption. My hon. friend mentioned one case which seems to be very worthy and he thinks that should be exempt. Other cases could be cited which would seem perhaps to be equally open to one's consideration. However, I realize that in our efforts, and in the efforts of our predecessors, to raise money it is quite possible some errors have been made. It is quite possible that there may_ be some room for criticism. I can assure my hon. friend that we appreciate what he has said, and if there are any other members who wish to join in the debate we shall be glad to welcome the attention and consideration that they may give to the subject. Our only desire, as I am sure he himself will realize, is to try and raise money and raise it in a manner that will be as little objectionable as possible to the public at large.
I do not think, I would respectfully submit to my hon. friend, that anything can be gained by having a committee because, as I I have said, the government must take the responsibility of raising taxes. I hope my hon. friend will on reflection see that he may accept the assurance that I give him that what he has said to-day, and what others have said-and indeed what others may yet say on the subject-will be received in the same spirit in which I know the criticism will be offered, and with every desire to meet objections as far as is reasonably possible.

We tried to get to the point where, at least in the majority of cases, it worked out that we would have such an impost that, while the resultant revenues would be large, yet in the particular instance of each case the amount would be so comparatively small that it would not be passed on. One particular matter I would like to draw to my hon. friend's attention is that when we have these sales taxes- and have them we must-they do not work out very fairly in connection with special,imposts on luxuries. In referring to the so-called luxury tax, the position was just exactly as I said when we introduced this tax into the House. The idea was that in some way we would stop the tremendous amount of luxurious buying in Canada, and' that we would in that way intercept, to some extent, the inevitable deflation that of necessity would come. Hon. members talk about deflation and blame the government for it. It is not a matter of government policy. Business deflates, and certainly in a place like Canada, next door to the great United States, when they de-
4 p.m. liberately embarked on that policy of deflation we had to follow. We buy our raw materials in the same markets. The prices are common, the purchases are common, the methods by which business is done are common and when they deflate we have to deflate. We wanted in some way or other to put the brakes on business to avoid to some extent the disastrous effects of deflation. Deflation is disastrous and it is a question which is the worse, undue deflation or great inflation. I am sure the effects of deflation are more disastrous than the effects of inflation. But knowing it was coming, we wanted to do something which would ease the shock, and these luxury taxes did ease the shock.
The manager of a large departmental shop met me in Ottawa about six months after the luxury tax had been imposed and when we were experiencing deflation and marked deflation. He said he called me all kinds of bad names, everything he could think of, when that tax was put on. He thought that I was everything I ought not to have been. Then he said "Do you know, when I stopped to think I wondered if you really were trying to make yourself the most unpopular man in the country, or trying to do a real service to Canada, and I came to the conclusion you were trying to do that real service, and having come to that conclusion, I knew the only thing you could be driving at was that you wanted to warn everybody not to buy. I stopped buying, and to-day my shelves are practically bare. If I had had the ordinary amount of stock, which in the ordinary methods of business I would have had on my shelves, I would have suffered very, very materially from this deflation; as it is today it is not hurting me." That was the reason that tax was put on. Immediately that

deflation had shown itself the tax was taken off, because it is really a tax that is not a fair one, a tax which singles out one particular activity as against all other activities. It is not a fair thing. I just want to give the House the one illustration that the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) has made plain. He spoke about the confectionery business and gave the names of some concerns engaged in that business. We had a luxury tax on candy. Candies were dear and they were being sold in great quantities.
That tax we took off, with all the rest of the luxury taxes but it was one of the last taxes we took off. We needed the money but the real underlying reason, apart from the unfairness of having two taxes upon one commodity, was that it is a tax which cannot be properly administered, for the simple reason that the foreigners,-and I am not using that word in the slightest degree offensively, because they make first class candies-are generally more or less uneducated people, and are more and more going into the candy business. In some of our smaller towns the candy merchants are Greeks and Italians. They go not only into the candy business but into the fruit business as well, and they are doing the business. They keep no books and I found it quite impossible to fairly and equitably enforce that double tax.
As I said in opening, I sympathize very, very deeply with my hon. friend. We must have the money; and must get it, but I hope he will see to it that this idea of double taxation, this special tax upon this activity or that activity, on top of the sales tax, is stopped, and I am inclined to think, from the representations which I know he must be receiving, that he has already come to the conclusion that it is an undesirable form of taxation.	.	.

And I would invite suggestions not only as to the way the tax ought to be imposed, but also as to the way it should be collected.

In this memorandum they say they have no objection to the sales tax being increased, if necessary. It is not the tax they are complaining of. They admit that the money has to be raised and that the sales tax is a means which can properly be made use of. It is simply a question of whether the tax is being collected in a fair and equitable manner, and it seems to me they have grounds for complaint as to the manner in which this tax is applied if one class of merchant has to pay a greater tax proportionately than another class of merchant, and that would seem to be the case in view of the illustrations which have been given by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. I quite appreciate the fact that the retailers, of course, would be inclined to get some other class to pay the tax insteajl of themselves. I have no doubt the same might be said of the manufacturers and of the wholesalers; there is always that difference of opin-

Special War Revenue Act
ion as to whom the taxes should be collected from. It seems to me that the suggestion made by the hon. member (Mr. Stevens) is a reasonable one, and that if you get taxation at the source you will not only derive a larger revenue but its collection will be less expensive.
There are differences of opinion, I admit, among the various classes that have to pay taxes, and all these different organizations have their own ideas as to the remedies which ought to be applied. If a committee of the House were appointed to consider this matter, which would not necessarily involve a great deal of expense, that committee might hear representatives of the various classes interested and might be prepared to make recommendations to the minister and to the government which would be deserving of consideration. We have had many committees appointed by the House in the last few years in the endeavour to adjust troublesome questions, and I think it will be admitted on all sides that all these committees have filled a useful purpose, and that some good, at least, has been derived from their deliberations. If, as the Minister of Cusf?ms says, this whole thing is propaganda on the part of certain officers of the Retail Merchants Association who desire to hold their jobs it would, of course, be unnecessary to have a committee; but if there are a number of problems involved-and the minister must know that there are a great many, not only in connection with the application of taxation and the specification of the sources from which the tax should be collected but also as to the manner in which that collection is made-it would seem only reasonable to agree to what the hon. member for Vancouver Centre proposes. I have heard that the machinery which is provided at the present time for the work of the department is not very complete. I do not know whether that statement is true or not, but possibly that machinery may be improved. That is another matter which might be considered by the proposed committee. I do not wish to take up time unnecessarily, but I would impress upon the minister the advisability of reconsidering his attitude in this matter. Let us have a committee and let that committee see if it can assist the minister, and the government also, in satisfactorily adjusting the difficulties which have presented themselves in connection with the application of this particular tax.

speechtext: Well, in view of the statement of the Minister of Finance a year ago in dealing with the sales tax, after the budget was introduced, may I direct his attention'and the attention of his colleagues to one item, and one item only, which I think has a very important bearing on the prosperity of the country, having to do with the reclamation of waste lands. It has been stated that means to pay the debt of this country must eventually come out of the soil. If that is the case, the greater the improvements made in the land of Canada the greater the returns must be. The item to which I would like t<^ direct the attention of the minister is that of field tile for drainage purposes. I know of cases during the past year where contracts have been let, and the tile purchased and delivered on the land, but no labour was available, and in consequence great loss has been sustained. In addition to that there is the further handicap in the shape of the sales tax which is imposed on this field tile, a tile which is used for reclaiming what are practically waste lands. I think splendid results came from the change which he then made, and I am satisfied that the use of field tile for reclamation purposes should also be encouraged rather than hampered by the sales tax.

speechtext:
There are one or two matters to which the hon. member for Vancouver Centre drew attention which have also been impressed upon me by different organizations in my district. The hon. member referred to the matter of the sales tax on books for public libraries. I have received from the librarian of the public library

of the city of Calgary, and also from the librarian of the city of Lethbridge, communications relating especially to this subject, in which the writers complained quite bitterly of the sales tax on the books which they purchased for these public libraries. The librarians referred to, therefore, urge very strongly that the sales tax be removed, to the end that the usefulness of these libraries may be extended, and the public given the full benefit to be derived from them. I hope that the Minister of Finance, to whom I am going to send these communications, will take this matter under advisement and see if he cannot arrange to relieve these public libraries from the burden of this extra taxation. When the budget was up last year and we were discussing this sales tax I presented a resolution or two from the labour organizations of the Lethbridge district resisting the increase in the tax that was made at that time. They are protesting particularly against the sales tax on the coarser lines of clothing and on boots and shoes. I hope the Finance Minister will carefully consider this matter also when he brings down his budget this year. I do not care to enter into details, but there are many matters in connection with the sales tax that should be adjusted. I believe these taxes are placing burdens upon the people of this country, and especially the class of people who can least afford to bear them, and I hope that every effort will be made this year to see that these articles of necessity are taken off the list to which the sales tax applies.
lion. H. H. STEVENS (Vancouver Centre): In view of the very courteous, and I think very frank, request of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau), the two members of the government particularly charged with the respective duties of imposing and collecting taxes, I am willing to halve the resolution withdrawn. But before asking you, Mr. Speaker, to make the request to the House that this resolution be withdrawn, may * I make myself clear on one point in regard to my suggestion? I admit that within the confines of a brief few moments' speech it is impossible to properly treat so important a subject, but I will just reiterate what I said a short time ago. I believe that the somewhat complex nature of the existing taxes could be very very much simplified if, instead of imposing a sales tax upon the various branches of trade-the dealer in the raw material, the manufacturer, the

wholesaler and the retailer-the taxes were imposed upon one branch, namely the manufacturer of the goods in their finished condition as issued to the consumer, and at the same time retaining the other features of this tax, namely, the sales tax imposed upon imports of an amount corresponding generally with the other tax. In addition to that I suggest that such a tax should be increased to an amount that would ensure the maintenance of the amount received. I know that the Minister of Finance understands what I have very imperfectly stated, and I would ask that, when he is giving consideration to this
5 p.m. problem, he would take that suggestion under advisement. I would like to tender another suggestion, that, perhaps between now and the time when the budget is considered by the Cabinet for presentation to the House, officers of the two departments might be detailed to give this matter special study and attention, and to hear the representatives of the manufacturers, the wholesalers and the retailers. In making this request I am quite aware that several delegations have waited upon the government and have submitted memoranda of various kinds, but I think if the two ministers would appoint from their departments one or two thoroughly expert individuals-and I know there are many such in the departments -to give immediate and definite study to the problem, with authority to hear these representatives and instructions to seek finality in the matter, that would certainly be better than even a parliamentary committee such as could make a report this session. These suggestions are given with a very sincere desire to solve a very difficult problem, and not with a desire to embarrass the government. speakeroldname: Mr. J. D. DRUMMOND (West Middlesex) moved:
speechtext:
Whereas the sheep-raising industry of this Dominion is suffering severely from restricted markets and inadequate returns received by the wool-growers engaged in the industry;
And whereas the present markets are further restricted by misrepresentation as to woollen products;
Therefore, be it resolved: That, in the opinion of this House, it is highly desirable that the government should bring down legislation that will adequately protect both producer and consumer by compelling manufacturers of goods sold as woollen goods to mark or label such goods in accordance with the composition thereof; showing plainly the percentage of virgin wool, shoddy, cotton or silk or other materials contained therein, and that importations of such goods be certified in similar or equally adequate manner.

Marking of Woollen Goods
He said: I hope that this resolution requires very little explanation. It is in reality something that has been before the people of the United States for two or three years known there as the "Truth in Fabric Act." The intention of the resolution is not to prevent the use of shoddy, because we realize that if that were done there would not be enough "woollen goods in the Dominion of Canada for the purpose for which they are needed, but, as the resolution itself states, to place the public in a position to know what they are buying. Permit me for a moment or two to take up the resolution as it pertains to the producers of wool. It is, of course, a fact that is well known to every agricultural man in the House, that the sheep industry in the Dominion of Canada is on the decline. The reasons for that may be several, but we believe it to be mainly the fact that the wool has not been sold at a price that would return an adequate profit to the wool grower. We believe that the producer of virgin wool should not be placed in the position where he is a competitor with the rag man or the producer of shoddy. To this end we ask that what is contained in the resolution be put into legislation: that is, that manufacturers be compelled to mark or label such goods as they manufacture in accordance with the composition thereof, showing plainly what is contained in those goods, whether it be a percentage of shoddy, or whether it be a percentage of silk, cotton or any other material. This is something that has been asked for by many sheep breeders' associations both in the Dominion of Canada and in the United States. It is something that has been asked for also in a number of newspaper editorials. I have a list of newspapers which since 1919 have taken up this matter and, so far as their influence can go, have ranged themselves behind it. It is not necessary for me to read them; suffice it to say that I have 32 press editorials from Canada and the United States in favour of legislation of this kind. I have also, from wool growers and live stock associations, the National Consumers' Association, etc., in the United States and Canada, some 60 resolutions that have been passed to the same end. I intend to be brief and for that reason I shall not read many of these resolutions, but I might read the following resolution passed by the Ontario Sheep Breeders' Association in Toronto on February 26 of this year.
That we, the members of the Ontario Sheep Breeders' Association, urge the Canadian government to enact fair and equitable legislation that will ensure "truth" in fabric; and in such an effort we pledge them our undivided support.
In view of the fact that the sheep industry is on the decline in Canada, I think I am only voicing the sentiments of most of those who are engaged in agriculture in this country when I say that this is deplorable from the farmers' standpoint, not only in the production of wool but in other ways as well. Those of us who have been engaged in agriculture all our lives, and who have for the greater part of that time had something to do with raising sheep, know that there is no means by which the eradication of weeds can be so successfully accomplished as by the pasturing of sheep. This is one reason why sheep raising should be encouraged in the Dominion.
I do. not think it is necessary for me to say much more from the point of view of the producers, but for a few moments I might consider the matter as it affects the consumers, because this is one of the things that do not affect any particular class. It affects, in fact, two classes, the consumers and the producers, who comprise the population of Canada. It is a fact that is well known to those who have given any study to the question that shoddy as used in the manufacture of cloth is sometimes worked over up to eight and ten times. In every process it is carbonized and the dress material and other undesirable elements are eliminated, leaving only the wool. I want to emphasize the distinction between virgin wool and shoddy, because one might go to buy a piece of cloth and be told that it was all wool, whereas it might be shoddy and the merchant might nevertheless be telling the truth. We do not want to eliminate the use of shoddy in the production of fabric, because there is not enough wool produced in Canada to provide more than one-third of the cloth necessary for the use of the people. It is therefore actually necessary that shoddy should be used in the manufacture of cloth. What we do ask, however, is that when it is used the percentage that is contained in the fabric shall be made known to those who buy it. When the United States government and, as well, if I am rightly informed, the government of Canada, were clothing their troops for overseas service, they made it obligatory on the part of those who provided cloth for the soldiers' clothes that they should state what percentage of virgin wool and what percentage of shoddy such cloth contained. If that was necessary in connection with the cloth provided for the soldiers' clothing, surely it is also necessary as regards the clothing that our people in general wear.



Marking oj Woollen Goods
This is a principle that has been applied and carried out in the Pure Foods Act. For instance, the manufacture of oleomargarine is not prohibited, but it is definitely laid down in our legislation that the people must know whether they are buying oleomargarine or butter. In the manufacture of maple syrup no one will for a moment say that the addition of cane sugar or any other ingredient is deleterious, but it is the function of the Pure Foods Act to safeguard the public by providing that they shall know whether what they are buying is pure or is an adulterated article. The same thing applies to milk. Nobody will say that the addition of water to milk makes it unfit for human consumption. But the Pure Foods Act clearly and distinctly lays it down that milk of a certain quality must be sold or the buyer must know what he is getting. I do not think it is necessary for me to go much further. I have a considerable amount of material which it would take me an hour or two to consider, but I have no desire to do so. I might refer before concluding to a bill that has been before the Senate of the United States for two years and which has been thrown out on both occasions. That bill is coming back this year with every prospect of being passed. Now, we: do not ask this parliament to pass a bill of that character, but it indicates what we are seeking. It provides:
. That every manufacturer of woven fabrics that contain wool, and of garments or articles of apparel made therefrom, shall. . . . cause the said woven fabric to be marked, and all garments and articles of apparel made therefrom shall be tagged in the manner hereinafter provided.
Now, I do not propose to lay down any lines on which this might be carried into effect, but it is something to which I hope the government will give their attention. I trust that something will be provided that will not only help those who are engaged in the important industry of sheep raising in Canada but will afford some protection to the consuming public.	*

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
The hon. member (Mr. Drummond) who has presented the resolution has introduced in the language of the resolution, a tariff issue that is familiar to many of the people of this country. He suggests that we provide for adequate protection. I should like to submit to my hon. friend that while we all share his views as regards the wisdom of providing the people of this cold country with woollen goods that are really woollen, and while the government are in sympathy with anything that will help to encourage

the sheep industry throughout the country, I am not sure how far the gentlemen who sit around him are prepared to follow him in this resolution. It seems to me that this is adequate protection to the limit. For while we are prepared at once to admit that parliament might enact legislation compelling our own manufacturers to visibly brand the products of their mills, I would ask my hon. friend what control have we over foreign manufacturers? If we, adopt this resolution, it simply means that we are handing over the whole business in question to the manufacturers of Canada and are keeping out the competition which we believe is in the best interests of our domestic trade.
There are many ways besides a customs tariff of protecting national industries. We have learned that truth ourselves. For man}' years our cattle were kept out of the British market because it was represented by the British cattle men that our stock was diseased. This was purely a pretence to protect the British cattle industry. We know to-day that certain of our industries are deprived of business in other countries because of restrictions by way of specifications governing contracts. I have in mind complaints that are now before my department. Canadian industries desired to tender for locomotives to be shipped to an overseas dominion, but the specifications framed by those who were able to control that business were such that our Canadian industries were shut out. Only last week we had brought to our attention the case of a manufacturer not far from Ottawa who had secured an order for 30,000 doors to be shipped to the United Kingdom. But he could not ship them because the carpenters there said, "You have not provided certain information as to what you pay for labour." No person is foolish enough to believe that this is done for any other object than to protect the particular industry affected.
If this resolution goes through in its present form, and it becomes an order to the government to bring in the legislation my hon. friend is asking for, it is in the last analysis the highest degree of protection. My hon. friend has debated the question. The government are desirous so far as possible of seeing that all goods sold throughout this country are what they are represented to be to the public, but I submit to him that in the interests of our people generally the government cannot accept this resolution because it is purely a measure of protection, worse even than any he would find in the customs house.

What has the government done along this line to protect the public?

Marking of Woollen Goods
The greatest protection the public can have is competition. This resolution would destroy competition.
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) absolutely and entirely mistakes the motives prompting the hon. member who has moved this resolution.
I am not attributing any motives to the hon. member; I am pointing out the possible results of the resolution if it goes through.

He may not
know it, but nothing is being done, so far as I am aware, to help that primary activity which ought to be great in this country-the production of Canadian wools. The subject has been discussed before. We had it up before the tariff commission time and again, when farmers showed what could be done, the kinds of wool that could be grown, and the like. We had it up in connection with our Marking Act. Of course, the present government threw it out.
What, the Marking Act?

It was something which was a little troublesome, something which made difficulties. Why, there is a firm in Scotland which turns out the best grades of tweed in the world, and it stamps every yard of its product with its name and a guarantee, as I recollect it, that it is composed entirely of pure wool. The thing can be done. Of course, it will be a little troublesome, of course the trade will come down and make trouble, of course the importers will come down and make trouble, and of course it takes time to convince people in the business of handling shoddy that this thing is right. But why attempt to dispose of the proposal by raising the*Rugaboo of protection?
That is what it is.
Does my hon. friend argue that the only shoddy sold in this country is the product of Canadian mills?

My hon. friend is indeed short of argument when he advances a question of that kind. Shoddy? Look at what you are getting through your customs to-day if you want to find shoddy. Let my hon. friend examine the imported article that he is so solicitous for if he wants to find shoddy. I can assure him he will find any quantity of it. The hon. minister says he wants to do everything for this industry that he possibly can-he wants to help the farmer,
59J
he wants to help the wool industry, he wants to see that when our people buy goods they may know what they are buying; and yet he will not do the one thing which would render it possible for them to know what they are buying.
This proposal is not anything new. The Marking Act of the United States covers it. That act is enforced when it is convenient; sometimes it is not convenient. But such an act can be enforced. My hon. friend says that the purpose of this resolution is absolute protection. I do not know why. I do not know why it is any harder for the foreign manufacturer to do what my hon. friend would say it is perfectly all right to make the domestic manufacturer do if it did not result in protection-to honestly state what is in his goods. He says, "We have got control over the domestic manufacturer; we can see that he is honest, we can see that in so far as his materials are concerned the Canadian purchaser will know what he Is buying." But he asks, "what control have we over these foreign manufacturers?" Equally great -greater control because it can be more easily enforced by my hon. friend, the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau). Why, all these imported articles have to come through his watchful department, and it is perfectly easy for him to see whether they are pure articles or not-that is, if it is required.
What would you do if they are not marked?

Well, I can tell the House what my hon. friend does when goods are not marked. He knows what to do with goods that his government want to have marked in connection with interests that they wish to protect. Why, they feel that it is necessary to mark pencils-one of the smallest-and^-mest-insignificant businesses in this country.
Everybody uses them.

An industry employing probably less men by many units than any other we could seriously discuss. But there is a pencil factory in Newmarket the owner of which was the chairman of the election committee of the right hon. Prime Minister.
Hear, hear. More power to his arm.

My hon. friend knows what to do when pencils try to get in that are not marked; they simply do not get in, that is all.

Marking oj Woollen Goods
Oh, they do. We mark them.
Yes, you hold them up and mark them at the shipper's expense.
How about printing and lithography?
The same thing about that as well. We thought all these things should be marked.
Oh, no.

Not on the basis of this man's politics or that man's politics, or with reference to the question whether he was chairman of the Prime Minister's election committee, but simply on the basis of what was right.
And that is why you suspended the Marking Act.

We wanted the Canadian public to know what they were getting. We wanted it not only on pencils but on cutlery, and everything. But no cutlery was being manufactured in that particular place; there was no knife factory there. The knife factory was in Kingston.
These are cutting remarks.
They happen, Mr. Speaker, to be true remarks.
Partly.
My hon. friend says, " partly ". Will he tell me wherein they are incorrect?
They are incorrect in this respect: My hon. friend stated that we did away with the Marking Act. His government suspended the act; it never was in force.
Now, let us try to get down to facts.
Hear, hear.

The Finance Minister threw away the Marking Act with a wave of his hand in his last budget. But it was found convenient later to hang on to something in order that these privileges might, be given. It was convenient to do it, and it was done.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says " hear, hear ". It was also convenient to give this protection, not to the wool producer, not to the maker of cutlery, but to this pencil manufacturer, and also to the lithographer.
(Sir Hairy Drayton.)
And printers.

And printers. It is right that lithography and printing, a first-rate business in this country, should be looked after, but other industries should also be looked after. My hon. friend has no difficulty whatever in looking after the lithographer, the printer, and the manufacturer of pencils.
Because they made a good case, and the others did not.
Well, here is a case being made for others.
I have not yet passed on it.
Then I hope my hon. friend will give to the wool industry and the farmers producing wool in this country the same measure of protection that he gives to the manufacturer of pencils.

Has the matter of the
pencils hurt my hon. friend more than anything else?

No, but I would like to see them all treated alike. My hon. friend cannot say that it is more important to have pencils made in Canada, even at Newmarket, than it is to grow wool on a thousand farms. He cannot say that the wool industry and the farming industry are not more indigenous to Canada than the making of pencils. If my hon. friend is going to see that the farmers get just as square a deal as the manufacturers of lead pencils in Newmarket, I am quite content to say nothing more upon the subject.
That is a matter of tariff, and I leave it to the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Speaker, I was surprised that the matter of protection was introduced into the discussion of this resolution. I did not understand that the motion was made primarily with the intention of asking for protection for the woo) growers. There is another class who need some protection-not tariff protection, but protection from the efforts of those who are selling an adulterated product for the pure article-and that class is the great unorganized mass of the people of Canada. They are the victims more than the wool growers. Everybody has to buy clothing. We go into a store and a dealer will say, "This is an all-wool article." But very few articles of clothing are one hundred per cent wool as they are sold for. The shoddy manufacturer will have in stock goods that are eighty per cent shoddy, and the adulterated article is sold as a pure wool

Marking of Woollen Goods
article. In this case, who is defrauded most, the buyer of the cloth or the wool grower? Why, the person who buys the cloth. And the beneficiary of the system is the shoddy manufacturer. Should this system be allowed to continue just for the benefit of a few shoddy manufacturers? I do not think so. The wool growing industry of this country is a very small one, but it could be one of our first industries if conditions were as they should be. Very few farmers raise sheep to-day; they have no encouragement to do so. If sheep were raised in greater numbers the result would be far-reaching in many ways. There would be more grain grown and sold; and surely we need larger production to take care of the overhead liabilities that confront us. Every basic industry should be given a square deal. We are not asking for protection, but we are asking for fair treatment. The Canadian Co-operative Wool Growers last year sold most of their wool in the United States, paying 15 cents a pound to get it there, and an equal amount of woollen goods was subsequently shipped back to Canada, the Canadian consumer paying the duty. What is the matter with our having the wool manufactured in our own country? There is something wrong, and I would like somebody who is wise on the subject to explain.
Now, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb), referring to the cattle embargo, pointed out that the contention that disease prevailed among our cattle was merely a pretence ; that it was protection our friends on the other side wanted. Well there have been a good many pretences by politicians to try to get by with something. In this case we are not asking that the wool grower should be protected at the expense of the consumer; in fact, if such protection was afforded it would be only the due of every consumer. The great unorganized masses have a claim on the -gftypmmiait t.hnt, all these grinds should he
marked. We have to sell our wheat, our oats, our flax, our hogs on this basis; they are all graded; why should not clothing be graded? Why should not the manufacturer have to mark on the goods what percentage of wool and what percentage of cotton or shoddy is in it? That would give the buyer a square deal, because the people cannot be good judges themselves. As far as the imported article is concerned, I think the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) is right, that it is easier to check up the importer than it is the home manufacturer, because you could very easily put a mark on the imported article. I very much hope that this resolution will receive the support of the House and become law.

I should like to express my sympathy with the motion before the House. I have watched the woollen industry in this country for thirty years or more now, and my father before me. He made it an outstanding item in his programme that the first thing Canada wanted was a woollen industry, so that our farmers might produce wool, and in the next place that our factories might make that wool into goods that could be used for clothing.
The only objection I have heard against the proposal made here to-day is that it is one instance more of a system of double-barrelled protection being introduced into this House. The mover proposes that there shall be protection to the wool grower and at the same time protection to the consumer who uses the wool. While it may be protection, and protection in the double sense, I am convinced from my experience in the past, and I have also been impressed by what the mover has said that the wool growing industry in this country is declining. I would like to see the growing of wool become one of the staple industries of this country, and I want to see our farmers encouraged by some kind of protection if protection is being applied to other industries in this country. It may be said that our friends here to my left are inconsistent. Perhaps they are and perhaps they are not, but whether they are or not, inasmuch as the principle of protection has been recognized and applied to many industries in this country, the farmers are entitled to their share of protection.
I also agree with the mover that this question is coming up in the United States, where the farmers' demands are growing, and are being recognized more and more. The outstanding thing in recent legislation at Washington was the putting through of a bill to provide a way for the farmers getting additional credit outside of the banks. I have not any doubt that the next Congress will pass a similar bill to that being urged here to-day, and that under their broad system of protection they will include the farmers as well as the manufacturers. I hope the government that we have in this House to-day, if they are not going to carry out their free trade principles but afford more or less protection, will apply the principle of protection to the wool growers as they are applying it to, some of the other industries, as was mentioned here to-day.
Again I say, I shall have much pleasure in voting for the motion and supporting it on this occasion, and later on if it comes up in

Marking of Woollen Goods
this House. The agitation will go on, and especially will the farmers continue an agitation for the recognition of the Wool growing industry in this country. It is more a basic industry than almost any other I know. Wheat growing may be a basic industry, as they say, but certainly wool growing is. Wool is grown in the West and in a large section of the province of Ontario, but it is a declining industry. I maintain that if there is any country competent to engage in the wool growing industry it is Canada, and if that industry is failing there must be something wrong. It may be within the compass of this parliament to apply a remedy to that grievance, and that grievance does exist. The question is now before parliament and now is the time to give some relief to the wool growers of Canada.

As I understand the resolution before the House, it is not asking protection for the farmers, but we would like to see encouragement given to the wool growers. We know that the sheep industry is dropping away in this country and that many of the farmers raising sheep consider that the wool, the product of their sheep, is scarcely worth taking off. We have known cases of farmers allowing the wool clip to lie over for one season, considering it scarcely worth while to draw it to market. So if this resolution is going to do anything to encourage the use of woollen goods in this country, it is going to help the farmers to that extent. I cannot understand how it is going to affect the manufacturer of shoddy goods. In no way will he be affected, nor will it affect any man or woman who wants to buy shoddy goods, nor the manufacturer who produces a mixture of cotton and wool or of some other materials, because the people will still be able to buy that class of goods if it is manufactured, and I presume that the manufacturers will still continue to manufacture it. But if this resolution becomes law the consuming public will be protected against buying an article that is not what it is supposed by them to be. It will put the consumer in a position where he will know what he is getting. If he buys woollen goods it will be marked woollen goods, and if he buys a mixture or shoddy he will know it as such. So I think this is a very important thing, not only to the wool growers of this country but also to the consumers who buy and use the goods. For these two reasons I am in sympathy with the spirit of the resolution, and hope that legislation will be introduced bringing it into effect so that the people of this country will know exactly what they are buying, and can get just exactly what they pay for.

I only intend to take a minute or two. I was rather surprised at the jocular manner in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) treated this resolution. It also surprises me to see how joyfully hon. members point to some member in this corner of the House and say that he is advocating protection.
You enjoy it.

Yes, because it is getting to be a joke. I can assure hon. gentlemen that it does not act like a red rag to a bull for us to hear the word "protection" mentioned. Perhaps there is a place for it. However, I do not see any signs of protection in this resolution. Perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce wants to adequately protect the people of this country from the cold weather by seeing that they get proper underclothing. I notice that there may be a little difficulty in connection with the working out of this resolution should it become law, but I think the principle is sound upon the whole, and that the difficulty referred to might be overcome. I feel greatly encouraged to see the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) taking up the wool industry and helping out the farmers who are engaged in the very laudable calling of raising sheep. I happen to be the proprietor of a fairly large flock of sheep and I am very much interested in the price of wool, but I do not know how this proposition might act. If you could convince me I was going to get a bigger price for my wool-well we will not say any more; but let us not even mention the word "protection" in regard to the selling and the buying of wool. I remember a little incident which occurred-I am rather afraid I mentioned this last year but I am going to repeat it because it is so good it is worth repeating. I happened to be selling wool and was unable to get enough for it to pay for the cost of shearing the sheep and carrying the wool to market. At that very time I went into a store to buy a small woollen cap. The clerk asked me $3.50 for a small cap. I looked rather suspiciously at him and asked him if he was not ashamed to ask such a price for a cap of that description, and he almost whispered to me "isn't it all wool?" You know it is rather trying on a man who is trying to raise sheep and sell wool to have to buy tweed caps. However, I survived the experience, and I am happy to say that the price of wool has greatly improved during the last year.
While I have this .opportunity I want to say to the farmers-I think the observation is applicable, perhaps to farmers throughout

the Dominion-that there is no better class of live stock to have on the farm at the present time than a few sheep; it is the best paying proposition we have in live stock to-day. With these few remarks I wish to state that I am going to support this resolution. I recognize there is a little "catch" in it, but that can be overcome and the principle itself is sound.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. KENNEDY (Glengarry and Stormont):
speechtext:
I was rather surprised at the
manner in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce received the suggestion of my hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Drummond). I would like to draw his attention to the fact that the mover of the resolution did not make the fact of the protection it will afford the wool-grower the main reason for his argument-that was more or less incidental to the argument which he presented. His main argument was that the people of this country were entitled to know the quality of the goods which they were buying.

I fear there has been a misunderstanding, I did not refer to it as protection to the wool grower. What I wished to make clear was that it was protection to the Canadian manufacturer, because he would have all the business.

I fail
to see the force of the minister's argument, because he would' not be placing the Canadian manufacturer under a less handicap than the manufacturer abroad who is sending his goods into this country; and I cannot believe but that the manufacturer in Great Britain, as well as the manufacturer across the line, would be willing to comply with the regulations in order to get his goods into this market. The increased demand for wool would largely come about in this way. The people, realizing the value of getting first -class goods, would buy more of them; there would be a greater demand and a greater consumption of the best quality of woollen . goods, which would result in a greatly increased demand for wool in this country. Why, our manufacturers now import large quantities of their wool from outside. I think, possibly, the greater quantity-yes much the greater quantity-comes from outside of Canada, so that there is absolutely no protection for the wool grower; and although there might be, perhaps, some little advantage to the Canadian manufacturer, I would suggest to the minister that it would be quite easy to overcome that by, reducing . the customs duty on manufactured woollens. There ;s no trouble in getting over a little difficulty of
that kind and therefore I would heartily support the resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Every grower of wool is familiar with the fact that the industry has got into low water since the war. Although there has been an improvement in the price of wool, nevertheless the industry is not yet by any means in a too flourishing condition. I have been, in common with my staff, casting about to see in what direction we could move to encourage this industry but I must confess that it never occurred to me that a means of rescue could be found in this way. There is no reason in the world why the home manufacturer's of woollen goods cannot comply with the conditions laid down and I think there are many reasons why they should. But I do not think that the imposition of these conditions on imported goods of this nature is practicable. I am not familiar with the importation conditions in regard to woollen goods, but I do know that in the case of certain importations with which I am conversant we are obliged by an understanding with the United States to accept their goods in the containers in which they are presented and they accept ours in return. I do not know whether these conditions apply to woollen goods or not but it would be manifestly unfair to impose conditions in the case of home manufactured goods and exempt from those conditions goods that are imported. This should be a matter for the customs and the finance departments to work out together. I think every member of the House must sympathize with the object of the resolution. We should be able to get at a solution of the difficulty somehow. But I understood from the Finance Minister that the thing would 1 be impracticable, it could not be carried into effect, and therefore, I ask, why pass this ..resolution? The Finance Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the Min- " ister of Customs know infinitely more about this matter than I do. I know something of the requirements of the sheep industry and of the condition it is in, but I am not familiar enough with this phase of the matter to speak as to the conditions to be imposed on the importation of woollen goods. If we impose these conditions on these goods of home manufacture and cannot impose them on imported goods of a like nature, look at the difficulty you are in. Let somebody who is -familiar with the business try to solve this riddle and then we are more likely to arrive at a satisfactory conclusion. However, there is no sense in advancing a resolution of this nature unless it can be complied with, and
Civil Service Act

my understanding is that it cannot be complied with, as affects the imported article.

speakeroldname: Hon. JACQUES BUREAU (Minister of Customs and Excise):
speechtext:
I do not look upon this as a question of protection although really that is involved. The marking of goods is not, in itself, a measure of protection but practically it works out that way. So much for that. Let me say that I am thoroughly in sympathy with the desire to help the sheep industry in this country. As the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) has rightly said, it is one of our industries that should be helped if that can be done. Now what is the purport of this resolution? It is set forth therein that our markets are restricted and that if we desire to help the sheep industry we must enlarge those markets. The resolution declares:
Whereas the sheep raising industry of this Dominion is suffering severely from restricted markets and inadequate returns received by the wool growers engaged in the industry:
And whereas the present markets are further restricted by misrepresentation as to woollen products.
That is the point we have to solve. How are we going to enlarge our markets ? The second part of the resolution states that:
It is highly desirable that the government should
bring down legislation that will adequately protect both producer and consumer.
If I understand the resolution correctly, the markets are restricted on account of the fact that misrepresentations are made. In other words, you have to deal with unscrupulous merchants or unscrupulous men who either manufacture or retail the wool that is produced by the farmers. That is the only thing that restricts our market. The suggestion is that the men who deal with the product he raises on his, farm, when it is converted into cloth or otherwise, are not honest in their representations. As the hon. leader of the Progressive party said, when they sell you a tweed cap they have to whisper in your ear, " It is all wool," because they are afraid to say it out loud. Does my hon. friend think that the marking of the goods is the remedy, and that it is an adequate remedy, instead of using the words " adequate protection " which we have heard so often in this House ? That is a debatable question. Another matter which I am most interested in is the question, how will it be possible to do it in a commercial way, or in a way which will not impede trade or prevent the free exchange of merchandise of this particular class ? My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance ( Sir Henry Drayton)-and when I say my hon. friend I emphasize the word " friend "-
Not the other word too ?

Oh, yes, he is a Sir. The word honourable sinks down to that.
In regard to the Marking Act my hon. friend wants to reproach me-and I think for once in his life he is unfair,

with putting lead pencils and printed and lithographed matter on the marking list.

I move the adjournment of the debate.
